endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: First, however, an upfront investment of time and effort is needed to map root causes and understand the specific needs of those experiencing the problem(s) via primary research.

endorsements.title: Commentary: Patient Perspectives on Artificial Intelligence; What have We Learned and How Should We Move Forward?
endorsements.quote: Patient stakeholders have different perspectives that can add value to both the identification and prioritization of healthcare research to which we want to apply AI [ 13 ].

endorsements.title: Recommendations for Successful Development and Implementation of Digital Health Technology Tools
endorsements.quote: The first step in developing DHTTs is to fully understand the specific health care challenge and associated knowledge gaps, with a focus on the patients’ and caregivers’ needs.

endorsements.title: Stakeholder-centric participation in large language models enhanced health systems
endorsements.quote: Incorporating stakeholder-centered methods, such as pre-design surveys and interviews, to identify and define specific healthcare problems early in the process ensures that solutions are not only innovative but also practically grounded.

endorsements.title: A participatory approach to deploy responsible artificial intelligence for diabetes prediction and prevention
endorsements.quote: Working collaboratively with our partnership table, in Phase 2, we complete a needs assessment to understand the context in which the diabetes AI tools will be implemented.

endorsements.title: A call for ethical, equitable, and effective artificial intelligence to improve care for all people with epilepsy: A roadmap. A report by the ILAE Global Advocacy Council and Big Data Commission
endorsements.quote: Concurrent early interactions with health care providers who can synthesize domain knowledge will allow developers to generate tools that are actually needed all while avoiding solutions that improve care at the expense of increased administrative and technological burden.

endorsements.title: A cautionary tale for AI and machine learning in psychiatry
endorsements.quote: Clinicians, AI researchers, and end-users (providers and patients) must work together to identify meaningful predictors, outcomes, and data collection strategies aligned with clinical needs [ 51 ].

endorsements.title: Moving beyond the benchmarks: Five foundational principles for meaningful AI evaluation in healthcare
endorsements.quote: The key is ensuring that at some point before deployment, researchers ask communities: ‘We can build this, but should we?’

endorsements.title: The ethical application of artificial intelligence in digital health: patients' knowledge, pulmonary hypertension, and the problem of misrecognition
endorsements.quote: Co-frame the problem with patients, and where relevant, caregivers, before ‘success’ becomes fixed in a specification.

commentary.bottom_line: No study in this evidence map tests whether engaging affected stakeholders before selecting an AI solution leads to tools that better address the actual problem. Support for R458 currently rests on one framework rated as a must and eight commentaries rated as should.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard. The nine endorsements consist of the CHAI guide and eight commentaries, which express expert agreement but supply no comparative data. Under GRADE conventions, consistent opinion cannot substitute for tested outcomes, so certainty about benefit cannot be rated.

One commentary describes a partnership table and needs assessment for diabetes AI tools, and another calls for co-framing problems with patients and caregivers, but neither commentary reports outcomes from that work. No supplied study measures whether early engagement changes tool fit for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy groups.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare AI projects with and without structured pre-selection stakeholder engagement, such as needs assessments, interviews, or pre-design surveys, and that measure whether the selected tool addresses the defined problem, gets used, and changes patient or workflow outcomes. Such studies should also report the time and staff cost of engagement.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested this practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups have no direct evidence on whether, or how, early engagement improves the fit of AI tools for them.
